items.title: Final Fantasy 14’s Most Unique Crossover Is Officially Returning This Week
items.summary: Celebrate the start of fall with Fall Guys
items.content:
By Willa Rowe Published Oct 6, 2026, 9:16 AM EDT Willa Rowe is a contributing writer at Polygon, covering games and entertainment. She is a New York-based journalist and critic whose work has been featured in Kotaku, Digital Trends, the A.V. Club, GamesRadar+, and more. She also co-hosts the Girl Mode podcast. News Celebrate the start of fall with Fall Guys

Image: Square Enix Final Fantasy 14 Sign in to your Polygon.com account Add Us Summary Generate a summary of this story Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Thread Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap Final Fantasy 14 is no stranger to collaborations. Square Enix's MMO has been running for over a decade and, in that time, has crossed over with other Final Fantasy titles , NieR: Automata , Monster Hunter, and more. None of these holds a candle to what I find to be the strangest, but perhaps most inspired collaboration in the game: Fall Guys . Luckily, the party game's multiplayer shenanigans are returning to Eorzea for a limited time.

Square Enix has announced that the Final Fantasy 14 and Fall Guys collaboration event will return beginning on Oct. 7 at 1:00 a.m. PDT. Warriors of Light will have just under three weeks to enjoy the festivities, as the event will conclude on Oct. 27 at 7:59 a.m. PDT. This will be the fifth iteration of the event, which was first held in 2023 and returned twice in 2024 and once in 2025.

To take part in the collaboration, players will need to accept the quest "Just Crowning Around" from the NPC Lewena in The Gold Saucer. To do this, you have to be at least level 15 and have completed the quest "It Could Happen to You." If you've played the collaboration before, you will be able to immediately resume playing the event's special Golden Saucer games.

Image: Square Enix Just like Fall Guys , the collaboration event is centered around participating in numerous multiplayer elimination games that resemble extreme obstacle courses. Blunderville, as the mode is called, consists of three stages, culminating in a single victor. Many of the games are exact recreations of those seen in Fall Guys .

Playing Blunderville awards you Manderville Gold Saucer Fame (MGF) based on your final rank in each match. The special event currency can be exchanged for various prizes at the MGF Trader in Blunderville Square. There are a lot of rewards to choose from, but the highlights are a pink bean minion, a set of Fall Guys -themed pajamas, and a pair of crowns to designate yourself as a winner. A full list of prizes and their required MGF is available on the collaboration's special site .

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

Final Fantasy XIV Haurchefant Nendoroid Debuts in 2027
items.summary: The Final Fantasy XIV Nendoroid of Haurchefant will join figures of Y'shtola and G'raha Tia next year.
items.content:
The next Final Fantasy XIV Nendoroid figure of FFXIV Heavensward character Haurchefant Greystone will launch worldwide in 2027. It will appear in every region at about the same time. It will debut in February 2027 in Japan for 7,900 yen . The North American launch window is Q1 2027, and it will be $53.99 here . It follows other items like the Chocobo Nendoroid already out worldwide .

As is common, Haurchefant comes with three face plates. Good Smile Company and Square Enix noted one is his “Splendid” smiling one, while the other two are a more subtle smile and determined face. He also comes with a Fortemps Kite Shield and Winglet sword, as well as hand parts for different poses.

He isn’t the only FFXIV Nendoroid to show up so far. Y’shtola Rhul , G’raha Tia , and Estinien Varlineau . We’re also expecting Emet-Selch and Yotsuyu Brutus ones.

The Final Fantasy XIV Haurchefant Greystone Nendoroid will show up in Japan in February 2027 alongside the Q1 2027 North American debut of the FFXIV Heavensward character. Pre-orders close on November 11, 2026. The game is available on the Switch 2, PS4, PS5, Xbox Series X, and PC.

items.title: Final Fantasy XIV Diesel Apparel and Merchandise Revealed
items.summary: Italian brand Diesel has released a new Final Fantasy XIV-themed collection of apparel and merchandise in Japan.
items.content:
A new merchandise lineup based on Square Enix’s Final Fantasy XIV has appeared courtesy of the Italian brand Diesel. The latter revealed it via its Japanese official website and social media account .

The premium brand sells a variety of items ranging from apparel to necklaces and phone cases. However, all of them cost more than ¥10,000. The most affordable ones are moulded cases for the regular and Pro versions of iPhone 17, both of which have the same price tag of ¥11,000 (~$69.80). Meanwhile, the most expensive item in this lineup is the FF-D-Barus Jacket , which costs a whopping ¥132,000 (~$837.85).

The median price of this collection is ¥23,100 (~$146.50), which falls on the T-Norm shirts with ten different back designs available. These designs are also available to view right below:

This collaboration adds yet another entry to the list of merchandise collections based on Final Fantasy XIV . In August 2026, Square Enix released the Emet Selch Earring and perfumes inspired by 21 in-game jobs. It also worked with its subsidiary Taito to bring back the Mini Lamp Quest icon magnets as arcade prizes, as well as Suntory to sell cans with sticker labels featuring the MMORPG’s characters via vending machines.

The Diesel x Final Fantasy XIV Capsule Collection merchandise is now available in Japan. The items are based on the MMORPG readily accessible worldwide on PC, PlayStation 5, PlayStation 4, Xbox Series X, and Switch 2 .

items.content:
Oct 02, 2026 at 11:30am ~ Nov 08, 2026 at 8:00pm

Diesel Art Gallery in Shibuya is hosting “Brave,” a free exhibition by collage artist Kosuke Kawamura, from Oct 2 to Nov 8. Held to mark the launch of a capsule collection from Diesel and the online role-playing game Final Fantasy XIV. The show features new collage works for display and sale, along with goods available only at the exhibition.

Kawamura is known for the main visual of the 2012 “Katsuhiro Otomo GENGA Exhibition” and the Oasis 30th anniversary logo. He has served as creative director of Uniqlo’s UT line since 2021.

Merchandise includes posters, acrylic keychains and clear files, plus T-shirts and hoodies from a three-way collaboration with the artist. The collaboration T-shirt is also sold at Diesel Shibuya and through the Diesel online store from Oct 2.

items.title: Meet The $13,000 Robot Toilet That Actually Comes To You
items.summary: I have always stared at Final Fantasy XIV Online from a safe distance. To be completely honest, it felt like…
items.content:
I have always stared at Final Fantasy XIV Online from a safe distance. To be completely honest, it felt like too big a task. The game has been running for over a decade, producing countless expansions, housing millions of dedicated players, and generating lore so deep it could easily fill a state library. Jumping in now felt a bit like starting a ten-season television series on the day of its grand finale. It is intimidating, to say the least.

However, the recent launch of the game on the Nintendo Switch 2 has completely shifted my perspective. The portable nature of the new console has opened a gateway for new players like me to finally jump in and experience what is widely regarded as one of the world’s best MMOs. The prospect of tackling this colossal universe from the comfort of the lounge room, or while travelling, was exactly the push I needed. After spending weeks immersed in its beautiful lore, I can confidently confirm that the Switch 2 version is an incredible entry point for newcomers.

Before we talk about how the game plays today, we need to briefly acknowledge its history. Final Fantasy XIV had a notoriously rocky start back in 2010. It was plagued by design flaws and performance issues that threatened to ruin its reputation completely. Rather than abandoning ship, Square Enix did something unprecedented: they brought in a new director, tore the game down, and rebuilt it from the ground up, launching the A Realm Reborn reboot in 2013. It is this rock-solid foundation that the Switch 2 version builds upon, delivering the full, uncompromised experience.

The narrative drops you into the land of Eorzea as a customisable hero during a time of intense geopolitical tension. Five years after a catastrophic war, the expansionist Garlean Empire was pushed back by the Eorzean Alliance. Now, the Empire is hungry for revenge and winding up for another grab at ultimate control. Amidst this brewing conflict, you receive a vision from Hydaelyn, a mysterious goddess of light. She names you her chosen champion and tasks you with finding six magical crystals to fend off an approaching darkness.

This initial premise sets the stage for the Hydaelyn-Zodiark Saga, a massive fantasy epic. It is a story bursting with intricate subplots involving various nations, factions, and memorable supporting characters. It is not just a game; it is a living, breathing world that you slowly become a part of.

Final Fantasy XIV follows a traditional MMO structure. You are given a massive open world to explore, dotted with Main Story Quests (MSQ), side missions, dungeons, and raids. As long as you stick strictly to the main questline, the game gently guides you through its core mechanics and introduces you to new areas at a very measured pace.

What the game does exceptionally well is its ‘Job’ system. In many modern RPGs, you choose a class at the beginning of the game and you are locked into that choice for the next hundred hours. Here, your character is wonderfully versatile. You can independently level up dozens of combat and non-combat jobs on a single character. Combat leans into the classic Active Time Battle (ATB) style, blending action with cooldown-based strategy. Every job has distinct mechanics. For instance, the Thaumaturge requires you to constantly shift between two passive states to balance your damage output and your magic regeneration. It keeps battles engaging and prevents combat from devolving into mindless button mashing.

The non-combat roles are equally impressive. If you decide to take up life as a Goldsmith, you do not just click a menu button and wait for a shiny new ring to appear in your inventory. Crafting is an active, strategic minigame where you must carefully balance progress and quality against the diminishing durability of your materials. It is highly rewarding and synergises perfectly with your combat classes, allowing you to craft better gear to tackle tougher foes out in the wild.

Another system I like is the control scheme. Translating a complex PC interface designed for a mouse and keyboard to a handheld console is no small feat, yet the controller UI is fairly intuitive. It takes a little time to learn, but the menus and hotbars are expertly adapted for the Switch 2, making navigation feel natural.

Of course, the experience is not without its flaws. The pacing can be incredibly jarring, particularly in the base game. The initial sixty-hour storyline acts as a massive exposition dump. You will spend hours scrolling through unvoiced text from non-playable characters to set up future conflicts. It asks for a lot of patience before the plot truly picks up steam, but that is what you sign up for when you jump into an MMO of this scale.

The game’s age occasionally shows. While the art direction is stunning, you will notice stiff character animations and simplistic environmental models. On the performance front, the Switch 2 handles the game reasonably well, but it is not flawless. In smaller areas while docked, the frame rate can touch 60 frames per second. However, for the vast majority of your journey (especially in handheld mode) it hovers around a stable 30 frames per second. It is a minor letdown, but the sheer scale and spectacle of the dungeon boss fights easily overshadow the technical limitations.

If you are wondering whether this massive undertaking is for you, consider your gaming history. If you enjoy the deep, methodical world-building and complex character interactions of The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt , combined with the endless, rewarding skill progression of a game like World of Warcraft or RuneScape , you will feel right at home here. Additionally, if you love the strategic, stat-driven combat of classic Final Fantasy titles but want it presented in a more modern, active format, this game perfectly bridges that gap.

Final Fantasy XIV Online is a massive commitment. With over a decade of content, updates, and expansions packed into the cartridge, it is entirely possible to pour hundreds of hours into Eorzea and still only scratch the surface. It demands your patience during its slow early hours, but the payoff is a rich, continually evolving RPG experience that very few other games can rival. The Switch 2 port is a technical marvel that makes this sprawling universe more accessible than ever before.

items.title: Final Fantasy XIV’s latest patch basically starts Evercold, but only gives you a short taste
items.content:
I know I said last time we’ve officially entered Evercold, but you can take that statement even more literally with patch 7.56. The MSQ for this patch is short but sweet, taking the Warrior of Light, Alphinaud, and Estinien to the fourth. There, we’re trapped on a deserted island, attacked by some strange machines, and saved by what is no doubt a teaser for the new ranged job to be revealed at the Tokyo Fan Fest. I won’t spoil it here, but it looks cool even if it isn’t exactly what I wanted. (I wanted something using Vanille’s whip staff thing from FFXIII, but maybe next time.) There’s unfortunately no dungeon or trial this time around, just two instanced battles, but both are a good time and interesting enough to engage you. The outfit you get at the end of the MSQ this time is also fantastic, and I’ve been using it as my Beastmaster outfit.

The focus of my time with this patch instead has been squarely on Beastmaster, the new Limited Job. As one of the few who love playing Blue Mage, I was stoked to have something similar again, and it seems a lot more people are enjoying this new job than did Blue Mage. That’s for good reason, as Beastmaster seems to focus way more on solo, open-world content instead of needing to go through party finder to get a group together for a dungeon. There is still some of that here, but most of the monsters you can tame are out in Eorzea.

More than anything, it’s nice to have something to do in these old zones again. I’ve been hunting down monsters to add to my besti-beastiery, fighting random mobs for experience, and running FATEs with other random players. That part alone is a lot of fun, but Beastmaster has its own unique gameplay style unlike any other job, even back when Summoner was actually a pet class. The basic loop for Beastmaster has you summon one of your three chosen monsters, then you and your companion attack an enemy to build up your respective TP bars. Once one of you reaches 100 TP, you can use a special color-coded attack, which will then reset your TP back to 0. Every monster only has one color attack, while you have all four at your disposal. To do some real damage, you need to follow up the first attack with the next in the sequence, shown going clockwise on your job gauge. So if you do a green move, your monster needs to use red, for example. Either one of you can start or end the combo too, but you still need to go in clockwise order to gain any bonus effects.

You’re not just waiting around to build up these combos, as there’s still a lot to consider in the moment-to-moment combat, even if it is overall slower-paced than the typical jobs in the game. When summoning a monster to the field, you gain the One with Nature buff, which allows you to use either Borrow or Tempered Release. Borrow lets you gain a special action based on the monster’s species for the duration they are on the field, while Tempered Release has your monster perform their unique skill. You can only use one per summon, so you need to choose wisely. You might want to borrow a cool dodge move that also grants you evasion up for a bit to dodge some incoming AoEs, or you might want your monster’s special healing skill for some more survivability overall. It’s a cool system even if it’s difficult to keep track of all the moving parts.

That difficult to keep track of theme continues in Beastmaster’s special solo content, the Crucible of the Unbroken. This is something of a rogue-like mode, where you move between spaces on a board game, with each space representing an encounter. You can pick a number of Beasties to join you on a board, but again, only three per battle, and all HP persists between encounters. You need to consider what monsters in your party will do the most damage or be the most survivable, when to use special items that grant healing, revives, or special buffs, and what temporary equipment you want to equip. It’s kind of a lot, but having only gone through the first board so far, it's a lot of fun too.

Overall, I’ve been having a blast with Beastmaster. While it can be a bit tedious to level at times, I’d prefer this be something that lasts me a good long while rather than speeding to the current cap of level 50. This’ll probably hold me over until Evercold at least, which is great because I just got all my other jobs to cap after my raiding group disbanded amicably, and I need things to do. Hope you enjoyed the read, and I’ll see you again next patch.

items.title: Review: Final Fantasy XIV on Nintendo Switch 2 is the best version of the game
items.content:
I have wanted to get back into Final Fantasy XIV for quite some time. I am a massive fan of everything it offers, from the art direction to the scope of the world and adventures that are held within it. I love the way that it handles narrative within the MMO format, and the massive range of locations to visit. I really, really love the music (I went to a FFXIV symphony and everything), and just generally the very Final Fantasy design of it.

Related reading: To think that I played this for the first time way back on the PlayStation 3. My thoughts back then.

But – and it’s a big but – Final Fantasy XIV is a MMO, and MMOs do demand a time commitment, both in terms of the raw hours you plug into it, and the frequency with which you need to play. Take a big break from an MMO, and it just becomes progressively more difficult to step back into.

I tried to get back into FFXIV once when I first picked up the ROG Xbox Ally . The device handled the game just lovely, but I’m not a frequent PC player, and so at some point I put the device down, took a long break, and just… let my subscription slip again.

I am, however, a frequent Nintendo Switch 2 player. By that I mean “daily”. And so now, with the game’s little icon sitting right there on my Switch 2 home screen, I’ve been logging in for at least a little playtime every day. I’ve already made significantly more progress than I did on the ROG.

Final Fantasy XIV plays just lovely on Switch 2, to start with that important point. The console’s screen is just large enough to be able to handle the very busy interface (it’s an MMO, it’s necessary) without distracting from the core action when you want to watch the fireworks. The game’s visual engine is just now ever-so-slightly showing its age with relatively primitive character models and textures – it has been going for something like 13 years at this point – but the art direction is still as stunning as ever, and I’ve loved revisiting my favourite parts of the world from my first playthrough.

Speaking of, I have started a totally fresh character and save file (I wouldn’t even be able to track down my original avatar from a decade ago, if she still exists on servers somewhere, even if I wanted to. I can’t remember my username, password, or the email address it was attached to). I love how it’s possible to play through all the base game and early expansions with NPCs, and not rely on parties of humans for the various dungeons. If you’ve ever played a FFXIV dungeon before, you’ll know that human allies tend to… well, race through it. One of the few unpleasant memories I have from my first playthrough of Final Fantasy XIV was getting to the very final dungeon of the base game and basically missing the whole thing (and being left behind) because I was trying to follow the story. The conclusion to literally dozens of hours of play.

Now, thanks to NPCs, you can enjoy most of the many expansions and all the stories within them at your own pace. And enjoy the typically excellent music, enemy layouts and dungeon design without feeling rushed, too. I even took time to take screenshots, which is one of my favourite ways to log my adventures in this game.

There is a downside, though. Because Square Enix wants to funnel players into the later expansions where, from their perspective, all the value to the players is, they’ve taken steps to streamline the earlier parts of the game, meaning that you accumulate experience points much (much) faster, and have to do far (far) fewer quests along the way. I have been exclusively undertaking the main quest line, with no side quests, let alone grinding, and my avatar is more than twice the minimum recommended level for any given quest or boss battle.

I understand why they did this, because otherwise it would be a truly intimidating, overwhelming task for a completely new player to get up to the newer expansions, but it means that those same players don’t get to spend enough time in parts of the world to really enjoy their contribution to the whole. The major cities are fine, but you’ll fly through little town areas where previously you’d spend a gaming session or two completing all the side quests. They’re barely blips and blink-and-you’ll-miss-them moments now, which really messes with the pacing for what was previously a truly wonderfully paced game that slowly walked you from one wonder to the next.

I don’t necessarily know what the solution is there, though if it were possible, I would have appreciated the option to toggle whether I wanted the accelerating levelling on or not.

Still, that’s my only gripe. The only other minor issue is that, when it comes to the chat, the Switch’s virtual keyboard doesn’t exactly allow for the same typing speed as a proper keyboard. I don’t even know if it’s possible to connect a Bluetooth keyboard to the Switch 2, as I haven’t tried yet, but even if it were possible, that would significantly undermine the portability of the experience. Currently I haven’t been social enough in FFXIV to require the chat function much, but I can see that becoming an issue later on in the game.

Those are only minor quibbles, obviously, set against a game that is hundreds upon hundreds of hours in scope, and now in an extremely portable and accessible format. FFXIV is a hobby all by itself, and now I can embrace and indulge it in full.
